issues.explanation: Occupation 'Student' is implausible for age 73 because 'Student' is flagged as implausible if age > 40.

For a natural-disaster trauma, 'People cycling' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless there is disaster-specific context, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other items do not provide a plausible link to bicycles/cyclists.
'Being alone with men' implies an interpersonal/assault-related trigger context that is not reflected in the trauma type or elsewhere in the profile, making it clinically incoherent here.

Avoidance of unfamiliar places due to inability to assess danger can occur in PTSD, but alongside the selected triggers it pulls toward an interpersonal/urban threat pattern rather than a natural-disaster pattern. This becomes problematic because the threat items are not meaningfully linked to the disaster-specific cues represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'being alone with men' is hard to reconcile as a primary trauma-linked trigger unless there is additional interpersonal trauma not represented elsewhere. The other trigger items are disaster-plausible (locations, relaxed state), so this item stands out as clinically incoherent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: 'People can't be trusted' suggests an interpersonal betrayal/assault formulation rather than a natural-disaster formulation. In the context of the rest of the profile, this appraisal does not connect plausibly to the disaster-linked threat and memory items and appears trauma-type inconsistent.

vignette:
Koa, a 46-year-old auditor of Oceania descent, presented to therapy with a quiet, almost resigned demeanor. His life had been irrevocably altered five years prior when a Category 5 cyclone, unprecedented in its ferocity, ripped through his coastal community in the dead of night. He remembered being home with his wife, sharing a rare moment of quiet happiness, when the power failed. The sudden, absolute darkness plunged them into chaos as the storm surge tore through their home. The memory of the event was so extreme it often felt unreal to Koa, difficult to believe it had actually happened to him. Yet, when the memories did intrude, they were intensely sensory; he could still experience a vivid olfactory recall of the damp, salty air mixed with splintered wood and decay, and sometimes even taste the metallic fear and seawater he had tasted during the event.

The loss of his wife and the sheer destructive power of the cyclone left Koa with a profound and unshakeable belief that he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him, a pervasive sense of helplessness that now colored every aspect of his life. This core conviction, coupled with the equally strong appraisal that the world was an inherently dangerous place, meant Koa’s internal alarm system was perpetually activated. Indeed, his deep conviction that the world was dangerous made him constantly vigilant for signs of peril, a state of hyper-arousal that was exhausting. He felt dead inside, an emotional numbness that had settled over him like a shroud, making it difficult to connect with others or feel joy.

This relentless monitoring of his surroundings, fueled by his negative appraisals, made him highly susceptible to intrusive memories. His mind would conjure fragmented images and sensations of the storm, which in turn could instantly amplify his feeling of impending doom. These vivid recollections often served to prime his system, making him even more reactive to his established triggers. For instance, the simple act of waking up in the dark at night would immediately plunge him back into the terror of the storm. Physical locations, especially those near water or damaged areas he encountered during his work, would trigger intense distress, and even moments of feeling happy or relaxed, perhaps while listening to music, could paradoxically trigger distressing memories, as that was exactly how he felt just before the disaster struck. Each time a trigger hit, it felt like confirmation of his belief that bad things were inevitable, reinforcing his profound sense of helplessness. His overarching sense that the world was dangerous also made him more susceptible to being triggered by mundane stimuli.

To manage the overwhelming distress from these frequent triggers, Koa developed a suite of maladaptive strategies. He started smoking heavily, a habit he hadn't had before, using it as a crude form of self-soothing when the anxiety became unbearable. He also began to avoid relaxing because it felt dangerous, fearing that any moment of peace would inevitably precede another catastrophe. This was a direct consequence of his belief that he couldn't stop bad things from happening. His job as an auditor often required him to travel to unfamiliar places, but now he actively avoided these assignments, convinced he couldn't adequately assess the danger in new environments. Furthermore, he found it nearly impossible to talk with others about the event or its aftermath, retreating into himself. These strategies, while offering fleeting relief, ultimately reinforced his core beliefs about his helplessness and the world's danger. By avoiding situations that might trigger him, Koa inadvertently strengthened the power of those triggers, never learning to cope with them. Furthermore, his avoidance behaviors prevented him from ever truly testing the perceived dangers, thus maintaining his heightened sense of threat.

The insidious cycle tightened. At work, an unusual silence in the office would make him feel something dangerous was about to happen, and if a report took longer than expected to arrive, he would immediately assume something bad was occurring. His constant vigilance, born from his belief that the world was dangerous, kept him in a state of high alert, and this heightened state easily gave way to intrusive memories, further fueling his sense of threat. The cumulative effect of these cycles had become unbearable. Koa sought help because the emotional numbness had grown so profound that he feared he was losing himself entirely, perpetually trapped in a world where danger lurked in every shadow and happiness felt like a prelude to disaster.
